01 / Hospitality / Self-initiated concept

Back to selected work
Aurelia

A beautiful villa can still be wrong for the trip. I designed and built Aurelia to help visitors find a Bali stay that fits their plans.

Live concept homepage, captured 25 September 2026.
Audience
People comparing Bali stays by location, pace, and practical fit.
My role
Independent product design and frontend build.
Collaborators
None.
Status
Concept. A request on the live site is not a confirmed booking.
View the live Aurelia concept
Design decisions
Start with the kind of day

Most stay sites start with a destination. I put the trip first: rest, explore, or work for longer. Area then narrows the list without replacing that intent.

Make the checks clear

Photos earn attention; access, noise, Wi-Fi, and privacy help decide. I kept those checks close to the stay and made the unconfirmed price and availability clear in the request.

Inside the concept
01 / 03
Skip to implementation notes

01

Give empty results an exit

Visitors can combine trip intention and area. If nothing matches, the page explains the result and Show all ten stays clears both filters. The search never ends at a dead end.

Live concept, 26 September 2026.
Open filters screenshot

02

Check a stay without losing the catalog

A detail overlay holds photographs, amenities, area, and Wi-Fi information. Closing it returns to the catalog, so visitors can compare another stay without starting over.

Live concept, 26 September 2026.
Open details screenshot

03

Make the request honest

Dates, Stay, and Contact form one request flow with a persistent summary. Back keeps the dates editable. The interface says plainly that a request does not hold a stay or confirm its final price.

Live concept, 26 September 2026.
Open request screenshot
Implementation notes

I separated browsing, stay details, and the request so each step has one job. Filters recover from zero results, the detail overlay preserves comparison context, and Back keeps entered dates available for editing.

The live concept demonstrates those interactions. It does not confirm real inventory or completed bookings.

Observed live flow

The recording shows the full loop: clear an empty result, inspect Wi-Fi, close the stay, advance the request, then return to edit the dates.

Recorded from the live concept on 26 September 2026 with sample dates. No request was sent.

02 / Finance / Client design project

Back to selected work
Paylecta

When money moves, merchants need to know what changed and what needs attention. I designed Paylecta's desktop and mobile dashboards around those decisions.

Original design presentation, June 2025. PDF page 1. Screen values are example content.
Audience
Merchants and small businesses managing money and customer records.
My role
Sole UI/UX designer for the dashboard, responsive screens, and visual system.
Collaborators
No other designers.
Status
Client design project, June 2025. The screens below are original design mockups.
Read the original Paylecta case study PDF
Design decisions
Give the balance a clear place

I put the balance first, then transactions and revenue. A pending-transaction notice points to work that needs action; the navigation keeps customers, invoices, and payouts distinct.

Keep detail and status together

Amounts, dates, and written states travel together. The mobile cards retain the essentials from the desktop records without squeezing a table into a phone.

Use a shared visual system

I used Plus Jakarta Sans, orange for the primary balance, neutral surfaces, and consistent card and status patterns. Repetition helps the screens read as one product.

Inside the design
01 / 03
Skip to implementation considerations

01

Keep the overview useful on a phone

On mobile, balance comes first, then transaction counts and revenue. The desktop account view gives profile, account, and funding details more room. I changed the hierarchy for the task, not just the screen width.

Source design mockups, June 2025. PDF page 4.
Open overview screenshot

02

Connect the summary to the records

Totals lead into a searchable customer table. Status and actions stay with each record; the customer form opens over the list so the user keeps that context.

Source design mockups, June 2025. PDF page 6.
Open customers screenshot

03

Make the payment state visible

An invoice preview sits beside the desktop editor. On mobile, overdue status, reminder, and activity stay together. Payout cards name each state beside its amount, so a color alone never has to explain what happened.

Source design mockups, June 2025. PDF page 7.
Open invoices screenshot
Implementation considerations

The mockups define the hierarchy, not transaction logic. A build would need validated inputs, a preview that matches the invoice sent, draft recovery, and clear success or failure feedback. Closing or retrying should not erase the work.

I would map desktop rows and mobile cards to the same record and actions, with written status labels, loading and empty states, and one definition for every financial amount.

What the evidence shows

These are original screens from my client presentation. They show the design and its intended states; I do not have a live product, working prototype, or measured business result to present.

The takeaway is simple: a useful dashboard connects the overview to the record someone can act on. The later gallery artwork is an illustration, separate from these source screens.

03 / Pet adoption / Self-initiated concept

Back to selected work
PawFriend

A pet is more than a photograph. I directed PawFriend's design and built an AI-assisted concept for comparing residents, saving a shortlist, and preparing for a visit.

Live concept captured 27 September 2026. Sample profiles with generated pet imagery.
Audience
Prospective adopters weighing personality, care, and household fit.
My role and collaborators
Design direction and ChatGPT-assisted implementation. No other design or build collaborators.
Status
Self-initiated concept
Evidence
Observed live interface and recorded interactions. No actual shelter inventory or adoption outcomes are established.
View the live PawFriend concept
View PawFriend source code
Design decisions
Put personality beside practical details

I kept age, breed, personality, and daily-life traits beside the photo. The details help someone compare a sample pet with their routine; they are not verified animal assessments.

Make saving visible and reversible

The heart, header count, confirmation, and drawer all reflect one shortlist. Removal is just as easy as saving, and the interface says the list stays on this device.

Explain the next step before commitment

I routed meeting interest to a checklist and FAQ, not an instant booking form. A real visit needs confirmed pet details and a conversation first.

From browsing to a first visit
01 / 03
Skip to implementation considerations

01

Browse beyond the portrait

The homepage features five pets. View all nine residents opens a grid with the same age, breed, personality, and meeting details for each sample profile. Comparison no longer depends on stepping through a carousel.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. Expanded sample catalog.
Open catalog screenshot

02

Keep a shortlist while considering the fit

Saving a pet updates the count and confirms the choice. The drawer holds the shortlist with a remove action on each profile. In the recorded browser, Milo and Luna survived a reload; removing Milo left Luna saved.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. Two saved sample profiles.
Open shortlist screenshot

03

Turn interest into preparation

Plan a meeting opens preparation guidance and an FAQ. It asks people to think about routines and questions for a first visit. It does not submit an adoption request or book a time.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. First-visit guidance.
Open prepare screenshot
Implementation considerations

The source stores favorites locally, filters stale IDs against the current catalog, and keeps the current selection if a storage write fails. The recording confirms persistence after a reload in one browser.

A real service would need a verified shelter feed, current availability, cross-device accounts if needed, and an explicit way to request, change, or cancel a meeting. This concept stops at preparation.

Observed live flow

The silent recording follows an empty shortlist through browsing, saving Milo and Luna, opening the drawer, and reading visit guidance. Both saves survive a reload; removing Milo leaves Luna.

Open the PawFriend live concept recording
What the evidence shows

The screenshots and recording show the live concept. The repository explains its implementation. Profiles and pet images are generated sample content, not shelter records; no adoption or measured outcome is claimed.

The lesson here is about pacing. Browsing leads to a reversible shortlist, then to preparation. It does not pretend that a saved heart means a meeting is booked.

04 / Food sharing / Client design project

Back to selected work
Munchpal

Food can be nearby and still hard to find or share. I researched and designed Munchpal's client prototype around local listings, requests, and donations.

Original client design presentation, PDF page 1. The screens show proposed app states.
Audience
People seeking food, people with surplus meals, and potential bulk donors.
My role and collaborators
Research, interviews, information architecture, user flows, wireframes, UI, and usability testing. No other design collaborators.
Status
Client design project. The sources document a prototype, not a verified public release.
Evidence
Original presentation and linked Figma prototype. The source's reported evaluation figures lack underlying records.
Read the original Munchpal case study PDF
Explore the original MunchPal prototype
Design decisions
Start with place and availability

I put city, search, and food categories before the listings. A request stays attached to its food item, where someone can judge what is offered and whether it is still available.

Separate asking from offering

Requesting starts from a listing. Offering starts from the central post action. Bulk donation has its own route. I kept these entry points distinct because each asks for different information.

Write the handoff states

The flow map names what follows a request or post. Notifications then distinguish new, accepted, and messaged states. This gave the prototype a clear handoff to design, without assuming the service was live.

From research to handoff
01 / 04
Skip to implementation considerations

01

Name the access and trust barriers

I interviewed Garda Pangan and worked through three concerns: food going unused, the discomfort of asking, and finding a nearby offer in time. The research summary shaped search, availability, and communication cues. The underlying responses are not published here.

Original case study PDF, page 4. The source's interview summary is not an independently verified research result.
Open research screenshot

02

Map both sides of the exchange

I mapped finding food, posting surplus, messages, donations, and community as separate paths. Request and post states connect to notifications, so the prototype can explain what happens after an action.

Original case study PDF, page 9. Designed flow; open the image to inspect the labels.
Open flow screenshot

03

Put nearby meals in context

City, search, and food categories narrow the nearby list. Each listing has a request action, while the central shortcut starts a post. The two sides of the exchange share navigation without sharing the same entry point.

Original case study PDF, page 12. Cropped from the high-fidelity interface section.
Open home screenshot

04

Show what happens after a request

Notifications distinguish a new request, acceptance, message, and donation report. Confirmation and accepted-request screens make the proposed handoff legible. They are design states, not records of completed pickups.

Original case study PDF, page 12. Designed feedback states, not recorded service transactions.
Open feedback screenshot
Implementation considerations

A working service would need live inventory, clear pickup arrangements, withdrawal when food is unavailable, and rules for food information, privacy, moderation, and notification delivery. The prototype specifies the path, not that infrastructure.

Garda Pangan took part in my interviews and appears in the bulk-donation design. Neither fact establishes a formal partnership or public integration.

What the evidence shows

The original PDF and Figma prototype show the research summary, flow, wireframes, interface, and proposed request and donation states. I ran usability testing, but the reported figures lack task-level records to verify them, so I have left the numbers out.

The design takeaway: finding food and offering it need separate starts, then shared status and communication. The sources do not show a released service or completed donation.

02 / Finance / Client design project

Back to selected work
Paylecta

When money moves, merchants need to know what changed and what needs attention. I designed Paylecta's desktop and mobile dashboards around those decisions.

Original design presentation, June 2025. PDF page 1. Screen values are example content.
Audience
Merchants and small businesses managing money and customer records.
My role
Sole UI/UX designer for the dashboard, responsive screens, and visual system.
Collaborators
No other designers.
Status
Client design project, June 2025. The screens below are original design mockups.
Read the original Paylecta case study PDF
Design decisions
Give the balance a clear place

I put the balance first, then transactions and revenue. A pending-transaction notice points to work that needs action; the navigation keeps customers, invoices, and payouts distinct.

Keep detail and status together

Amounts, dates, and written states travel together. The mobile cards retain the essentials from the desktop records without squeezing a table into a phone.

Use a shared visual system

I used Plus Jakarta Sans, orange for the primary balance, neutral surfaces, and consistent card and status patterns. Repetition helps the screens read as one product.

Inside the design
Skip to implementation considerations

01

Keep the overview useful on a phone

On mobile, balance comes first, then transaction counts and revenue. The desktop account view gives profile, account, and funding details more room. I changed the hierarchy for the task, not just the screen width.

Source design mockups, June 2025. PDF page 4.
Open overview screenshot

02

Connect the summary to the records

Totals lead into a searchable customer table. Status and actions stay with each record; the customer form opens over the list so the user keeps that context.

Source design mockups, June 2025. PDF page 6.
Open customers screenshot

03

Make the payment state visible

An invoice preview sits beside the desktop editor. On mobile, overdue status, reminder, and activity stay together. Payout cards name each state beside its amount, so a color alone never has to explain what happened.

Source design mockups, June 2025. PDF page 7.
Open invoices screenshot
Implementation considerations

The mockups define the hierarchy, not transaction logic. A build would need validated inputs, a preview that matches the invoice sent, draft recovery, and clear success or failure feedback. Closing or retrying should not erase the work.

I would map desktop rows and mobile cards to the same record and actions, with written status labels, loading and empty states, and one definition for every financial amount.

What the evidence shows

These are original screens from my client presentation. They show the design and its intended states; I do not have a live product, working prototype, or measured business result to present.

The takeaway is simple: a useful dashboard connects the overview to the record someone can act on. The later gallery artwork is an illustration, separate from these source screens.

03 / Pet adoption / Self-initiated concept

Back to selected work
PawFriend

A pet is more than a photograph. I directed PawFriend's design and built an AI-assisted concept for comparing residents, saving a shortlist, and preparing for a visit.

Live concept captured 27 September 2026. Sample profiles with generated pet imagery.
Audience
Prospective adopters weighing personality, care, and household fit.
My role and collaborators
Design direction and ChatGPT-assisted implementation. No other design or build collaborators.
Status
Self-initiated concept
Evidence
Observed live interface and recorded interactions. No actual shelter inventory or adoption outcomes are established.
View the live PawFriend concept
View PawFriend source code
Design decisions
Put personality beside practical details

I kept age, breed, personality, and daily-life traits beside the photo. The details help someone compare a sample pet with their routine; they are not verified animal assessments.

Make saving visible and reversible

The heart, header count, confirmation, and drawer all reflect one shortlist. Removal is just as easy as saving, and the interface says the list stays on this device.

Explain the next step before commitment

I routed meeting interest to a checklist and FAQ, not an instant booking form. A real visit needs confirmed pet details and a conversation first.

From browsing to a first visit
Skip to implementation considerations

01

Browse beyond the portrait

The homepage features five pets. View all nine residents opens a grid with the same age, breed, personality, and meeting details for each sample profile. Comparison no longer depends on stepping through a carousel.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. Expanded sample catalog.
Open catalog screenshot

02

Keep a shortlist while considering the fit

Saving a pet updates the count and confirms the choice. The drawer holds the shortlist with a remove action on each profile. In the recorded browser, Milo and Luna survived a reload; removing Milo left Luna saved.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. Two saved sample profiles.
Open shortlist screenshot

03

Turn interest into preparation

Plan a meeting opens preparation guidance and an FAQ. It asks people to think about routines and questions for a first visit. It does not submit an adoption request or book a time.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. First-visit guidance.
Open prepare screenshot
Implementation considerations

The source stores favorites locally, filters stale IDs against the current catalog, and keeps the current selection if a storage write fails. The recording confirms persistence after a reload in one browser.

A real service would need a verified shelter feed, current availability, cross-device accounts if needed, and an explicit way to request, change, or cancel a meeting. This concept stops at preparation.

Observed live flow

The silent recording follows an empty shortlist through browsing, saving Milo and Luna, opening the drawer, and reading visit guidance. Both saves survive a reload; removing Milo leaves Luna.

Open the PawFriend live concept recording
What the evidence shows

The screenshots and recording show the live concept. The repository explains its implementation. Profiles and pet images are generated sample content, not shelter records; no adoption or measured outcome is claimed.

The lesson here is about pacing. Browsing leads to a reversible shortlist, then to preparation. It does not pretend that a saved heart means a meeting is booked.

Saving a pet updates the count and confirms the choice. The drawer holds the shortlist with a remove action on each profile. In the recorded browser, Milo and Luna survived a reload; removing Milo left Luna saved.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. Two saved sample profiles.
Open shortlist screenshot

03

Turn interest into preparation

Plan a meeting opens preparation guidance and an FAQ. It asks people to think about routines and questions for a first visit. It does not submit an adoption request or book a time.

Live concept, captured 27 September 2026. First-visit guidance.
Open prepare screenshot
Implementation considerations

The source stores favorites locally, filters stale IDs against the current catalog, and keeps the current selection if a storage write fails. The recording confirms persistence after a reload in one browser.

A real service would need a verified shelter feed, current availability, cross-device accounts if needed, and an explicit way to request, change, or cancel a meeting. This concept stops at preparation.

Observed live flow

The silent recording follows an empty shortlist through browsing, saving Milo and Luna, opening the drawer, and reading visit guidance. Both saves survive a reload; removing Milo leaves Luna.

Open the PawFriend live concept recording
What the evidence shows

The screenshots and recording show the live concept. The repository explains its implementation. Profiles and pet images are generated sample content, not shelter records; no adoption or measured outcome is claimed.

The lesson here is about pacing. Browsing leads to a reversible shortlist, then to preparation. It does not pretend that a saved heart means a meeting is booked.

04 / Food sharing / Client design project

Back to selected work
Munchpal

Food can be nearby and still hard to find or share. I researched and designed Munchpal's client prototype around local listings, requests, and donations.

Original client design presentation, PDF page 1. The screens show proposed app states.
Audience
People seeking food, people with surplus meals, and potential bulk donors.
My role and collaborators
Research, interviews, information architecture, user flows, wireframes, UI, and usability testing. No other design collaborators.
Status
Client design project. The sources document a prototype, not a verified public release.
Evidence
Original presentation and linked Figma prototype. The source's reported evaluation figures lack underlying records.
Read the original Munchpal case study PDF
Explore the original MunchPal prototype
Design decisions
Start with place and availability

I put city, search, and food categories before the listings. A request stays attached to its food item, where someone can judge what is offered and whether it is still available.

Separate asking from offering

Requesting starts from a listing. Offering starts from the central post action. Bulk donation has its own route. I kept these entry points distinct because each asks for different information.

Write the handoff states

The flow map names what follows a request or post. Notifications then distinguish new, accepted, and messaged states. This gave the prototype a clear handoff to design, without assuming the service was live.

From research to handoff
Skip to implementation considerations

01

Name the access and trust barriers

I interviewed Garda Pangan and worked through three concerns: food going unused, the discomfort of asking, and finding a nearby offer in time. The research summary shaped search, availability, and communication cues. The underlying responses are not published here.

Original case study PDF, page 4. The source's interview summary is not an independently verified research result.
Open research screenshot

02

Map both sides of the exchange

I mapped finding food, posting surplus, messages, donations, and community as separate paths. Request and post states connect to notifications, so the prototype can explain what happens after an action.

Original case study PDF, page 9. Designed flow; open the image to inspect the labels.
Open flow screenshot

03

Put nearby meals in context

City, search, and food categories narrow the nearby list. Each listing has a request action, while the central shortcut starts a post. The two sides of the exchange share navigation without sharing the same entry point.

Original case study PDF, page 12. Cropped from the high-fidelity interface section.
Open home screenshot

04

Show what happens after a request

Notifications distinguish a new request, acceptance, message, and donation report. Confirmation and accepted-request screens make the proposed handoff legible. They are design states, not records of completed pickups.

Original case study PDF, page 12. Designed feedback states, not recorded service transactions.
Open feedback screenshot
Implementation considerations

A working service would need live inventory, clear pickup arrangements, withdrawal when food is unavailable, and rules for food information, privacy, moderation, and notification delivery. The prototype specifies the path, not that infrastructure.

Garda Pangan took part in my interviews and appears in the bulk-donation design. Neither fact establishes a formal partnership or public integration.

What the evidence shows

The original PDF and Figma prototype show the research summary, flow, wireframes, interface, and proposed request and donation states. I ran usability testing, but the reported figures lack task-level records to verify them, so I have left the numbers out.

The design takeaway: finding food and offering it need separate starts, then shared status and communication. The sources do not show a released service or completed donation.
